positions/wesleyan-quadrilateral/oneLine: Scripture is primary, but it is interpreted with the help of tradition (especially the early church), reason, and Christian experience of the Spirit's work.
positions/wesleyan-quadrilateral/coreCla: Scripture is the primary and final authority (‘a man of one book’).
Christian antiquity and the Church of England's formularies help read Scripture rightly.
Reason is God's gift for understanding and applying Scripture.
Experience, especially the witness of the Spirit and assurance, confirms Scripture's truth in the believer's life.
positions/wesleyan-quadrilateral/origin: Implicit in John Wesley's sermons and writings (1740s–1780s), building on Anglican appeals to Scripture, reason and tradition (Richard Hooker); named and systematised by Albert Outler in the 1960s and adopted in the United Methodist Book of Discipline (1972; revised 1988 to stress Scripture's primacy).
positions/wesleyan-quadrilateral/stronge: It describes how believers actually interpret Scripture.
It values the Spirit's present work while keeping Scripture primary.
It encourages a generous, ecumenical reading of the church's tradition.
The geometric image suggests four equal authorities; experience and reason can override Scripture in practice (Outler himself regretted the term).
Experience is subjective and culturally shaped.
Reformed critics see it as a departure from sola scriptura.
positions/wesleyan-quadrilateral/respons: Methodists emphasise that Scripture is primary and the others are interpretive aids, as the 1988 revision of the Discipline states.
Wesley tested experience by Scripture throughout his ministry.
positions/wesleyan-quadrilateral/consequ: Shaped Methodist, Holiness and Pentecostal hermeneutics.
Became a focal point in recent United Methodist debates on sexuality and authority (leading to the 2022–24 separations).
positions/neo-orthodox-word-of-god/name: Neo-orthodox view: Scripture as witness to the Word
positions/neo-orthodox-word-of-god/oneLi: The Word of God is primarily Jesus Christ; Scripture is the human witness to him, which becomes God's Word when God speaks through it, and preaching is the Word proclaimed.
positions/neo-orthodox-word-of-god/coreC: Revelation is God's self-revelation in Christ, not information in propositions.
Scripture is a fully human, fallible witness that God freely uses to speak.
The Bible ‘becomes’ the Word of God in the event of revelation by the Spirit.
Natural theology and religious experience cannot reach God; only God's free revelation can.
positions/neo-orthodox-word-of-god/origi: Karl Barth's Epistle to the Romans (1919/1922) and Church Dogmatics I/1–2 (1932–38), with Emil Brunner and the Barmen Declaration (1934), in reaction against liberal theology.
positions/neo-orthodox-word-of-god/stron: It centres authority on Christ himself, as the Bible does.
It accepts critical scholarship while recovering a strong doctrine of revelation.
Its resistance to Nazi ideology (Barmen, 1934) showed the force of confessing Christ as the one Word of God.
Evangelicals argue it makes Scripture's authority dependent on an event, not intrinsic to the text.
Liberals argue it is an arbitrary fideism that refuses rational scrutiny.
Catholic and Orthodox critics see it as lacking an account of the church's role in interpretation.
positions/neo-orthodox-word-of-god/respo: Barthians answer that Scripture's authority is God's free, faithful use of it — a fact grounded in God, not in the reader's experience.
They argue that recognising the Bible's humanity honours the incarnational pattern of revelation.
positions/neo-orthodox-word-of-god/conse: Dominant in mid-20th-century Protestant theology and ecumenism.
Influenced the Barmen Declaration and the Confessing Church.
Renewed interest in Barth's theology of Scripture among some evangelicals.
positions/inner-light/oneLine: Christ, the Light who enlightens everyone (John 1:9), speaks directly in the heart; the Spirit who gave the Scriptures is the primary authority, and Scripture is a true but secondary rule.
positions/inner-light/coreClaims/0: Immediate revelation by the Spirit continues and is available to all.
positions/inner-light/coreClaims/1: Scriptures are a declaration of the source, not the source itself (Barclay, Apology, Proposition 3).
positions/inner-light/coreClaims/2: Discernment takes place in the gathered meeting waiting in silence.
positions/inner-light/coreClaims/3: Outward rites and a paid ministry are unnecessary.
positions/inner-light/origin: Anticipated by Spiritualist reformers (Caspar Schwenckfeld, Sebastian Franck); founded by George Fox's preaching (from 1647; Pendle Hill vision 1652) and systematised by Robert Barclay's Apology (1676).
positions/inner-light/strongestArguments: It honours the promise that the Spirit will guide into all truth and write God's law on hearts.
It avoids bibliolatry and clerical control of interpretation.
It produced remarkable ethical fruit: early Quaker leadership in abolition, prison reform and peace witness.
positions/inner-light/strongestObjection: Without Scripture as a final check, private revelation becomes subjective and divisive (the James Nayler episode, 1656).
Reformers argued that the Spirit binds himself to the Word.
Later liberal Quakerism moved far from Christian orthodoxy, which critics attribute to this principle.
positions/inner-light/responses/0: Early Quakers held that the Spirit never contradicts the Scriptures, and practised corporate discernment.
positions/inner-light/responses/1: Evangelical Friends emphasise Scripture alongside the Light.
positions/inner-light/consequences/0: Quaker silent worship and non-hierarchical governance.
positions/inner-light/consequences/1: Influenced Pentecostal and charismatic emphasis on immediate guidance, and liberal religious individualism.
positions/marcionite-canon/oneLine: Christian Scripture should consist only of an edited Gospel (Luke) and ten letters of Paul, purged of Jewish ‘interpolations’; the Old Testament belongs to the lesser Creator-God, not the Father of Jesus.
positions/marcionite-canon/coreClaims/0: The God of the Law (just, wrathful) is different from the good Father revealed by Jesus.
positions/marcionite-canon/coreClaims/1: Only Paul truly understood the gospel; the other apostles judaised it.
positions/marcionite-canon/coreClaims/2: The Gospel and Paul's letters must be corrected to remove Jewish additions.
positions/marcionite-canon/coreClaims/3: The Old Testament is not Christian Scripture.
positions/marcionite-canon/origin: Marcion of Sinope, a wealthy shipowner, was excluded from the Roman church in 144 and founded a widespread church with its own canon (Euangelion and Apostolikon) and Antitheses.
positions/marcionite-canon/proponentsOth: Marcionite churches (extant in Syria into the 5th century)
positions/marcionite-canon/strongestArgu: It took seriously the newness of the gospel and Paul's contrast between law and grace.
It solved, in its own way, the moral difficulties of some Old Testament texts.
It offered a clear, fixed list of authoritative books.
positions/marcionite-canon/strongestObje: Jesus and the apostles constantly appealed to the Old Testament as God's Word.
Its ‘corrections’ are arbitrary editing (Tertullian: he used ‘the knife, not the pen’).
Separating Creator from Redeemer undermines the goodness of creation and the incarnation.
positions/marcionite-canon/responses/0: Marcionites claimed their texts were the original, uncorrupted versions.
positions/marcionite-canon/consequences/: Spurred the mainstream church to define its own canon of both Testaments.
Adolf von Harnack (1921) controversially suggested the church might drop the Old Testament — an idea repudiated, especially after the Holocaust.
positions/protestant-canon/oneLine: The Old Testament canon is the 39 books of the Hebrew Bible (the 24 books of the Jewish canon, counted differently); the deuterocanonical books (‘Apocrypha’) may be read for example of life but not to establish doctrine.
positions/protestant-canon/coreClaims/0: The Old Testament canon is that of the Jewish people, to whom were entrusted ‘the oracles of God’ (Romans 3:2).
positions/protestant-canon/coreClaims/1: Jesus' reference to ‘the law, the prophets and the psalms’ reflects the Hebrew canon.
positions/protestant-canon/coreClaims/2: Jerome and other Fathers distinguished canonical from ecclesiastical books.
positions/protestant-canon/coreClaims/3: The New Testament canon is the 27 books shared by all major traditions.
positions/protestant-canon/coreClaims/4: The Apocrypha is useful (Luther, Thirty-Nine Articles 6) or merely human (Westminster 1.3).
positions/protestant-canon/origin: Based on Jerome's ‘Hebrew verity’; Luther's Bible (1534) placed the Apocrypha in an appendix; Reformed confessions (Gallican 1559, Belgic 1561, Westminster 1647) excluded it from the canon; the British and Foreign Bible Society stopped printing it in 1826.
positions/protestant-canon/strongestArgu: It matches the canon of first-century Judaism as reflected by Josephus (Against Apion 1.8) and the Hebrew Bible.
Many Fathers (Melito, Origen's Hebrew list, Athanasius, Jerome, Gregory the Great) distinguished the extra books.
Some apocryphal books contain teaching (prayers for the dead in 2 Maccabees 12) Protestants believe conflicts with Scripture.
positions/protestant-canon/strongestObje: The early church's Bible was the Septuagint, which included the deuterocanonical books; New Testament writers allude to Wisdom and Sirach.
Councils (Hippo, Carthage) and most Western Fathers, including Augustine, accepted the broader canon.
Luther's critique of James, Hebrews, Jude and Revelation shows doctrinal criteria shaping canon decisions.
positions/protestant-canon/responses/0: Protestants answer that the regional councils of Hippo and Carthage were not ecumenical and that Jerome and others dissented.
positions/protestant-canon/responses/1: Allusion does not establish canonicity (Jude cites 1 Enoch, which most do not accept).
positions/protestant-canon/consequences/: A visible difference in Bibles between Protestants and Catholics/Orthodox.
Doctrinal disputes over purgatory and prayers for the dead partly depend on it.
positions/catholic-deuterocanon/name: Catholic canon (73 books, with the deuterocanon)
positions/catholic-deuterocanon/oneLine: The canon includes Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, 1–2 Maccabees and Greek additions to Esther and Daniel as fully inspired Scripture, as defined at Trent.
positions/catholic-deuterocanon/coreClai: The deuterocanonical books were part of the Septuagint used by the apostolic church.
The church's tradition, councils (Rome 382 per the Decretum Gelasianum's attribution, Hippo 393, Carthage 397, Florence 1442) and Trent (1546) recognised them.
The church, not the Jewish rabbinate after Christ, determines the Christian canon.
positions/catholic-deuterocanon/origin: Augustine and the North African councils; Pope Innocent I's letter to Exsuperius (405); the Council of Florence (Decree for the Copts, 1442); defined dogmatically at Trent, Session IV (1546).
positions/catholic-deuterocanon/stronges: It reflects the Bible actually used by most early Christians.
Hebrews 11:35 appears to refer to the martyrs of 2 Maccabees 7.
Continuity with the broad Western consensus from Augustine to the Reformation.
Jerome, Gregory the Great and Cardinal Cajetan doubted the books' canonicity.
Jesus and the apostles never cite them explicitly as Scripture.
Trent defined the canon in a polemical context, after a millennium of ambiguity.
positions/catholic-deuterocanon/response: Catholics answer that Jerome deferred to the church's judgement and translated the books.
The absence of explicit citation also applies to several protocanonical books (Esther, Song of Songs).
positions/catholic-deuterocanon/conseque: Catholic Bibles include 73 books; doctrinal support for prayers for the dead and purgatory.
Ecumenical Bibles (e.g. NRSV) print the deuterocanon in a separate section.
positions/eastern-orthodox-canon/oneLine: The Old Testament follows the Septuagint, including the Catholic deuterocanon plus 1 Esdras, 3 Maccabees, the Prayer of Manasseh and Psalm 151 (with 4 Maccabees in an appendix); the canon has never been closed by a single ecumenical decree.
positions/eastern-orthodox-canon/coreCla: The Septuagint is the Church's Old Testament, used by the apostles.
The ‘readable’ books (anagignoskomena) are received for reading in church, with some theological distinction from the Hebrew-canon books in some Orthodox writers.
The canon is defined by liturgical use and conciliar reception (Trullo 692; Synod of Jerusalem 1672).
positions/eastern-orthodox-canon/origin: Inherited Byzantine practice; affirmed by the Council in Trullo (692), which endorsed earlier lists, and the Synod of Jerusalem (1672) against Protestant views.
positions/eastern-orthodox-canon/stronge: Continuity with the Septuagint of the apostolic church and Byzantine liturgy.
It reflects a canon shaped by worship rather than polemics.
The lack of a precise, universal list leaves ambiguity.
Protestants raise the same objections as to the Catholic deuterocanon.
positions/eastern-orthodox-canon/respons: Orthodox writers argue that the Church's lived use is a sufficient criterion and that precision is a Western concern.
positions/eastern-orthodox-canon/consequ: Orthodox Bibles differ slightly among Greek, Slavonic and Georgian traditions.
